newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Clark moots working party on mandatory superannuation.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Clark moots working party on mandatory superannuation.

text.p: Labour leader Helen Clark on Tuesday hinted Labour was willing to have New Zealand First's compulsory superannuation policy referred to a working party.
She said the multi-party accord, which NZ First has not signed, had set the level of the pension where people could live in dignity.
"That raises the question as to why people should have to compulsorily save on top of it.

"Clearly it is something not envisaged by the present accord parties. Nobody would have difficulty putting it in front of a working party and talking about it further," Clark said in a transcript of a television interview provided by her office.
"But if we are paying NZ super at an adequate level for people to live on why require them to make private provision above that?" Clark said.
Nationalist NZ First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and is running parallel talks with conservative National and centre-left Labour over the shape of the next government.

Clark said Reserve Bank governor Don Brash's warning on Monday that tax cuts may have to be deferred if there was a net increase in government spending were aimed at the caretaker National Party government as much as anyone.

"Our response is that Dr Brash's warning is directed at National as much as anyone, because the Nats have insisted on wide-ranging tax cuts for next year, and would have to make social spending concessions to do a deal with NZ First."
Labour has said the planned July 1, 1997 tax cuts would not proceed, but would be revamped and deferred until April 1998.

She said there was no question there would be more social spending under a new government, because Labour's policy provided for it and National would have to agree to more spending if it did a deal with NZ First.
Clark said the talks were going well, were worthwhile, amiable and discussed many issues frankly.
"We would like to come to a deal with them (NZ First) because we think their policies are more in line with ours than theirs (National's)."
She said when Labour and NZ First's policies were lined up they were similar.
Parliament must meet no later than December 13, but the leaders of the three parties to the talks have said a decision on the new government may not be reached by then.
